Kozienice Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kozienice, Poland

Not demolished. Kozienice's Jewish community is documented from 1607, and from the 18th century the town was the seat of the Kozhnitz Hasidic dynasty. The cemetery itself predates that, first mentioned in a royal privilege granted by King Władysław IV in 1633, and grew through several expansions. In 1814 the town's first Hasidic rebbe, Yisroel Hopstein - the Kozhnitzer Maggid - was buried here beneath an ohel later shared by his descendants. By 1921, Kozienice's 3,811 Jews made up over half the population; most were murdered at Treblinka in 1942, and the cemetery was devastated during the war, its stones used to reinforce roads. After liberation, Jewish Committee activists reburied exhumed victims here, including 32 people interred in 1949. Poland ordered the cemetery closed in 1957, but restoration efforts since the 1980s - including a rebuilt ohel funded by Rabbi Mendel Reichberg in 2004 - have kept the site fenced and maintained, with a women's gallery and Holocaust memorial standing alongside surviving fieldstones.
